text: People are central to good manufacturing practice.
Every person whose activities can affect product quality needs
to understand their assigned responsibilities.
Clear reporting lines, appropriate staffing,
and suitable supervision support consistent execution.
Staff must follow approved procedures,
record work accurately, and report abnormal conditions.
GMP is not only the responsibility of the quality department,
it depends on coordinated action across the site.
Personnel should receive initial and continuing training
relevant to their duties.
Training may include GMP principles,
job-specific procedures, hygiene, safety,
and contamination control.
The organization should evaluate whether personnel
can perform assigned tasks competently,
using methods appropriate to the task and risk.
A training attendance record alone
does not necessarily demonstrate practical competence.
Retraining may be needed when procedures change
or performance gaps are identified.
Personal hygiene helps reduce the risk of contamination.
Personnel should follow site rules for health reporting,
hand hygiene, protective clothing,
and restrictions on items brought into manufacturing areas.
Hygiene expectations depend on the activity
and contamination risk.
For example, personnel handling exposed product
require controls appropriate to the manufacturing environment.
Site procedures should clearly explain what to do
when a hygiene concern is identified.
Gowning is a controlled process,
not simply putting on a garment.
The clothing type, gowning sequence,
changing room arrangements, and entry controls
depend on the area classification and operations.
Personnel should be trained in the approved
gowning procedure and any applicable
qualification requirements.
In sterile manufacturing,
gowning controls are particularly important.
This introductory lesson does not replace
detailed aseptic gowning qualification or annex one training.
Personnel behavior can affect contamination control
even when equipment and rooms are qualified.
Follow approved movement restrictions,
material flows, and entry rules.
Avoid unnecessary activity and interactions
that could disturb controlled conditions.
Do not touch exposed product contact surfaces
without appropriate controls.
If an unexpected event occurs,
stop or secure the activity as required
and follow the site escalation procedure.
Good habits help sustain a controlled state.
Contamination and mixup risks can arise
from incorrect materials, poor segregation,
inappropriate handling, and unclear identification.
Personnel should verify material and equipment status
before use.
Follow line clearance procedures where applicable
and respect area and campaign controls.
Labels and records should support identification
and traceability.
When an item or status is uncertain, do not guess.
Seek clarification and document the concern
according to procedure.
Supervisors should ensure that personnel
understand their tasks and that required controls are followed.
GMP records should identify who performed
or checked an activity when required.
Entries must reflect the actual work
and should not be backdated or fabricated.
Observation, coaching, and periodic review
can help identify training needs.
A culture that supports timely reporting of mistakes
and near misses contributes to product quality
and patient protection.
Imagine an operator entering a controlled manufacturing area
who notices that the required gowning step was missed.
The appropriate response is not to continue silently.
The operator should follow the site procedure,
which may require stopping, leaving the area,
regounding, and reporting the event.
Any potential impact on operations or product quality
must be assessed by authorized personnel.
The key principle is to identify, contain, document,
and address the issue rather than conceal it.
